oneLineAnswer: An antiviral medicine that can shorten and ease some herpes virus infections.
whatItIs: Acyclovir is an antiviral medicine. It is a synthetic nucleoside analogue, a lab-made molecule that resembles one of the natural building blocks of DNA. It is active against herpes viruses, including herpes simplex types 1 and 2 and varicella-zoster virus. The same medicine is also spelled aciclovir. Products listed in the sources include tablets, capsules, an oral liquid, skin creams and ointments, and an injection.
whatItDoes: Acyclovir is selective. A viral enzyme called thymidine kinase switches it on mainly inside infected cells.
The active form stops the virus from copying its DNA, so the infection spreads more slowly.
This eases and shortens outbreaks. It does not cure these infections, which stay in the body for life.
The oral forms are approved for shingles, genital herpes and chickenpox.
A prescription cream is approved for cold sores on the lips and face in people aged 12 and older.
howPeopleUseIt: The oral forms are taken at home. Some people take a short course for one episode.
Others take acyclovir continuously for months or years to reduce repeat outbreaks.
Labels stress starting as soon as symptoms appear. Nothing covers treatment begun later than 72 hours.
Creams and ointments stay on the skin. The cold sore cream is only for the lips and face.
Acyclovir also comes as an injection.
The oral labels reviewed are marked as prescription only.

commonSideEffects: In genital herpes treatment trials, nausea and vomiting were the most frequent side effects reported.
In a year-long trial of continuous oral acyclovir, nausea and diarrhea were the most frequent reported side effects.
In shingles trials, malaise, a general feeling of being unwell, was the most frequent side effect reported.
In chickenpox trials, diarrhea was the most frequent side effect reported.
With the cold sore cream, local skin reactions at the application site were reported by 5% of people in trials.
seriousSigns: The oral label lists kidney failure, in some cases fatal, as having been observed with acyclovir therapy.
A clotting and blood disorder called thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura has occurred, with deaths, in people with weakened immune systems.
Reported nervous system effects include confusion, hallucinations, tremor, seizures and coma.
The label says these effects may be more marked in older adults and people with kidney problems.
Severe skin reactions, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, have been reported.
Allergic reactions including angioedema and anaphylaxis have been reported.
whoShouldAvoid: People who have had a hypersensitivity reaction to acyclovir or valacyclovir should not use it, the oral label states.
The cold sore cream is only for the lips and face. It should not go in the eye or inside the mouth or nose.
The label says the dose must be adjusted for people with reduced kidney function.
Safety and effectiveness of the oral forms in children under 2 years have not been established.
The cream is not established in children under 12, or in people with weakened immune systems.

interactions: Probenecid, given with intravenous acyclovir, raises acyclovir levels in the body.
It also lengthens acyclovir's half-life, the time for half of it to leave the body.
The label advises caution with other medicines that can harm the kidneys.
That combination may raise the risk of kidney problems or short-lived nervous system symptoms.
pregnancyAndChildren: Acyclovir cream is barely absorbed through the skin. That label says it is not expected to reach a fetus. The same label says decades of use in pregnancy have not shown a raised risk of birth defects or miscarriage. Swallowed acyclovir does reach breast milk, and the older oral label advises caution during nursing. The oral forms are not established for children under 2. The cream is approved from age 12, and safety below 12 is not established.
whatWeDoNotKnow: Most of this record comes from product labels, not from independent reviews written for the general public.
The label records no data on whether acyclovir stops genital herpes from passing to a partner.
For shingles, the label records no data on treatment started more than 72 hours after the rash appears.
For chickenpox, the trials treated people within 24 hours of the rash. Later treatment was not studied.
The label states that the link between laboratory susceptibility results and a person's actual response is not established.
The cream's effect in people with weakened immune systems has not been established.
No source we fetched summarised in plain language how much acyclovir helps an individual outbreak.
We found no NCCIH page for acyclovir, and the LiverTox monograph was not reachable from this environment.

gaps: Only the titles and identifiers of the ClinicalTrials.gov records were read, so no trial result or outcome is reported here.
The LiverTox monograph for acyclovir could not be fetched: the NIDDK and NCBI book pages returned a bot check or a 404.
NCCIH has no acyclovir page, and its herpes simplex page returned a 404, so no NCCIH material is cited.
No allowed source gave a patient-friendly estimate of how much acyclovir shortens a typical outbreak.
The evidence comes almost entirely from labels from one regulator, so the record is not independently corroborated outside the United States.
The cold sore cream evidence refers to the brand-name label (Zovirax) and its generic equivalent; results for other topical products were not reviewed.
summary: This record covers what acyclovir is, what the labels say it does, how people use it, its recorded side effects and cautions, and the gaps the fetched sources leave open.
